Count regression: rate ratios between groups

Source: R/cntreg.R
cntreg.Rd

Fits a log-linear model of a count on a group, with adjustment columns, an exposure and clusters, by Poisson and negative binomial maximum likelihood, and reports the incidence rate ratio (IRR) of each group against the reference with its interval. The same model serves counts of people, placements, days or deaths in the cells of a published table and counts per person or per area.

Usage

cntreg(
  y,
  grp = NULL,
  adj = NULL,
  expo = NULL,
  clus = NULL,
  ref = NULL,
  gee = FALSE,
  cadj = TRUE,
  level = 0.95
)

Arguments

y

The counts: finite numbers from 0, not all 0; or a clpre list from clprep(), whose elements fill the arguments by name (arguments given here override them).

grp

The group of each count: labels (a factor by its levels, text or numbers by their sorted values), at least two groups.

adj

NULL or adjustment columns: a data frame or list of columns, a numeric matrix, or one vector, one value per count. Factor, text and logical columns enter as indicators of each level but the first; give a number such as a year as a factor for one effect per value.

expo

NULL or the exposure of each count (person-days, population): positive numbers; its logarithm is the offset.

clus

NULL or the cluster of each count (institution, region, year): labels, at least two clusters.

ref

The reference group: a label or a position; the first group by default.

gee

TRUE to fit the exchangeable GEE as well (needs clus).

cadj

TRUE for the G / (G - 1) factor on the cluster-robust variances.

level

The confidence level of the intervals: one number strictly between 0 and 1.

Value

An object of class cntreg, a list: irr, a data frame with one row per fit and group (fit, term, irr, lo, hi, p, sep); coef, every coefficient of every fit on the log scale (fit, term, est, se, z, p); fit, one row per model (fit, loglik, aic, theta, setheta, alpha, iter, conv, rank); ref, the reference group; n, the number of counts; ncl, the number of clusters (0 without clus); and level.

Details

The Poisson fit takes the steps of stats::glm() (iteratively reweighted least squares from y + 0.1, stopping when the relative change of the deviance is below 1e-8), and the negative binomial fit (variance mu + mu^2 / theta) those of MASS::glm.nb(): theta by maximum likelihood and the coefficients in turn. A column of the design that the columns before it explain (an adjustment level the group determines, say) is aliased and dropped, as R does: its coefficients are NA.

With clus, each fit also gets cluster-robust (sandwich) standard errors, rows "poiscl" and "nbcl": (X'WX)^-1 (sum_g U_g U_g') (X'WX)^-1 over the clusters' scores U_g, times G / (G - 1) for G clusters when cadj (the default of sandwich::vcovCL(); cadj = FALSE gives the independence GEE variance of 'geepack'). With gee = TRUE the Poisson model is also fitted by generalised estimating equations with an exchangeable working correlation (row "gee"), as geepack::geeglm(corstr = "exchangeable") estimates it.

Intervals are Wald intervals on the log scale, exp(est +- z se), with z the normal quantile for level. sep flags a ratio whose group or reference has no counts at all: the estimate then runs off towards 0 or infinity and its interval means nothing.

Counts need not be whole numbers (a median duration, say): the estimating equations are those of the Poisson pseudo-likelihood, and the log-likelihood uses lgamma(y + 1), where stats::glm() reports an infinite AIC.

References

Venables, W. N. and Ripley, B. D. (2002). Modern Applied Statistics with S, 4th ed. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-0-387-21706-2

Liang, K.-Y. and Zeger, S. L. (1986). Longitudinal data analysis using generalized linear models. Biometrika, 73(1), 13-22. doi:10.1093/biomet/73.1.13

Cameron, A. C. and Miller, D. L. (2015). A practitioner's guide to cluster-robust inference. Journal of Human Resources, 50(2), 317-372. doi:10.3368/jhr.50.2.317

Examples

# placements by group in eight institutions over three years
d <- data.frame(
  n = c(12, 30, 8, 25, 14, 41, 9, 22, 11, 35, 7, 28),
  female = rep(c("no", "yes"), 6),
  year = factor(rep(c(2021, 2022, 2023), each = 4)),
  inst = rep(c("A", "B", "C", "D"), each = 2, length.out = 12)
)
cntreg(d$n, d$female, adj = d["year"], clus = d$inst)
#> cntreg: 12 counts, 4 clusters; reference no
#> rate ratios (95% intervals):
#>     fit term      irr       lo       hi            p   sep
#>    pois  yes 2.967213 2.219882 3.966137 2.036053e-13 FALSE
#>      nb  yes 2.967220 2.211509 3.981170 4.108785e-13 FALSE
#>  poiscl  yes 2.967213 2.610266 3.372972 4.107025e-62 FALSE
#>    nbcl  yes 2.967220 2.610217 3.373050 4.296535e-62 FALSE
#> negative binomial theta 581.5672; AIC Poisson 74.68582, negative binomial 76.67518
# rates: a count per person-days of exposure
cntreg(c(5, 12), c("a", "b"), expo = c(1000, 1500))
#> Warning: cntreg: the negative binomial fit failed (theta has no finite estimate); its rows are NA.
#> cntreg: 2 counts; reference a
#> rate ratios (95% intervals):
#>   fit term irr       lo       hi         p   sep
#>  pois    b 1.6 0.563681 4.541576 0.3772454 FALSE
#>    nb    b  NA       NA       NA        NA FALSE
